preamble: The voiceless dental fricative [θ] becomes the postalveolar [ʃ] through palatalization, usually next to high front vowels or glides, or through mergers in which the interdental joins a sibilant series. Proto-Semitic *θ became Hebrew š [ʃ] while Arabic kept [θ]. In Pre-Proto-Algonquian, *θ was replaced by *š before *i, *iː and *y. Some Upper Tiyare dialects of North-Eastern Neo-Aramaic changed θ to š after a contracted *ay and in the ending *-iθa. In Mapudungun, replacing /θ/ with [ʃ] is part of an expressive (diminutive, endearing) palatalization.

examples.note: Regular merger of *θ with *š in Canaanite (Phoenician šlš too); Arabic keeps [θ] in ثلاث, and Akkadian has šalāšum.
After /ɛ/ from the contracted diphthong *ay (Talay 2008, as cited by Khan 2023).
In the feminine ending *-iθa of final-weak roots; both environments involve a high vowel, or historically one.
A regular palatalization in the proto-language, parallel to *t > *č in the same position (Goddard 1979). Massachusett continues the alternation as /n/ ~ /s/.
Expressive palatalization marking diminutive or affectionate meaning, recorded by Moesbach (1962); dentalization works the other way for pejoratives.

sources: Khan, G. (2023). Interdental consonants in North-Eastern Neo-Aramaic dialects. Kervan 27(2). https://doi.org/10.13135/1825-263X/8225
Molineaux, B. (2025). Affective coronal alternations in Mapudungun: Sound symbolism, change, and morpho-phonological structure. Journal of Linguistics 62(1). https://doi.org/10.1017/S002222672500012X
